title: The endgame: the weighted prime sum and its remainder, the one-sided criterion (Landau), the choice of the second scale, and the statements and assembly of Theorems A, B and C
summary: PrimeError defines the weight λ_{d,M}(ν) = Λ(ν)(1 − (ν/d)) on ν ≡ 1 mod M and the remainder R_{d,M}(x) of its weighted sum, proves the finite-sum identity used by the data, and shows that v ↦ R_{d,M}(e^v) is polar with residues given by orders of zeros of L-functions. OneSidedCriterion turns a one-sided bound R_{d,M}(x) ≤ x^(β−1), for all primes d of a class, into a zero-free half-plane Re s > β (Landau's lemma, applied with a prime d of the class whose quadratic twists of all characters modulo M have no zero in a box to the right of β; the artifact proves that such a d exists from its own zero-density estimate for quadratic twists), and finds in every window [t, t²] a second scale u where R − X·R′ ≤ e^(−t). ShortAndEnough defines the main amount, the remainder rem(D) and the index, bounds the height per row by the choice of the level prime, writes rem(D) through R_{d,N₀} and R_{d,1}, and proves Theorem A (short forms) and Theorem B (enough forms) from the seesaw identity, the size and divisibility of the chains of lifts, and the filling theorem. LongForms proves Theorem C (integral forms are long) by heights and the product formula, and combines A and B into one family.

members.name: lambdaClass
members.text: The weight of the prime sums. For a natural number d that is prime (instance `Fact (Nat.Prime d)`), a natural number M and a natural number ν: λ_{d,M}(ν) = Λ(ν)·(1 − χ_d(ν)) if ν ≡ 1 mod M (that is, (ν : ℤ/M) = 1), and λ_{d,M}(ν) = 0 otherwise; Λ is von Mangoldt's function (Mathlib's `vonMangoldt.residueClass`) and χ_d(ν) = (ν/d) ∈ {−1, 0, 1} is the Legendre symbol, i.e. the quadratic character of ℤ/d (`chiK d`), read as a real number. Λ(ν) ≠ 0 only for prime powers ν = p^j (j ≥ 1), so the congruence ν ≡ 1 mod M is a condition on p^j, not on p, and χ_d(p^j) = χ_d(p)^j: the factor 1 − χ_d(ν) is 0 when χ_d(p) = 1; when χ_d(p) = −1 it is 2 for odd j and 0 for even j; and it is 1 when p = d. The definition allows every prime d. Only for d ≡ 3 mod 4 (as in the later criterion, where d ≡ 7 mod 8) is χ_d the quadratic character of ℚ(√−d), so that χ_d(p) = −1 means that p is inert in ℚ(√−d); for d = 5 and p = 3, (3/5) = −1 although 3 splits in ℚ(√−5).

imports.name: IsPolar
imports.lean:
def IsPolar (E : ℝ → ℝ) (r : ℂ → ℂ) := Measurable E ∧ ∃ C Φ, Meromorphic Φ ∧ (∀ v ≥ 0, |E v| ≤ C *
  v.exp) ∧ (∀ s, 2 < re s → Φ s = ∫ v in Ioi 0, E v * ((1 - s) * v).exp) ∧ AnalyticOnNhd ℂ (fun s ↦
  (s - 1) * Φ s) {s | 1 ≤ s.re} ∧ ∀ ρ, 0 < ρ.re → (𝓝[≠] ρ).Tendsto (fun z ↦ (z - ρ) * Φ z) (𝓝 (r ρ))
imports.text: IsPolar(E, r) for E : ℝ → ℝ and r : ℂ → ℂ: E is measurable and there are a real C and a meromorphic Φ : ℂ → ℂ with |E(v)| ≤ C·e^v for v ≥ 0, Φ(s) = ∫_0^∞ E(v)e^((1−s)v) dv for Re s > 2, (s − 1)Φ(s) analytic near every point of Re s ≥ 1, and (z − ρ)Φ(z) → r(ρ) as z → ρ, z ≠ ρ, for every ρ with Re ρ > 0. Since Φ is a function defined at s = 1, the product (s − 1)Φ(s) vanishes at s = 1, so the analyticity says that Φ has no pole at 1 (off s = 1 it agrees with a function holomorphic near 1), as the source's doc comment says; read in ordinary notation without that value, '(s − 1)Φ(s) analytic' would still allow a simple pole.

imports.text: Landau's lemma, in this form: for E : ℝ → ℝ and r : ℂ → ℂ with IsPolar(E, r), a real β > 0 with Re r(x) ≥ 0 for every real x > β, and E(v) ≤ e^((β−1)v) for all sufficiently large v: r(ρ) = 0 for every complex ρ with Re ρ > β. literature.verdict: corollary of Widder's theorem (The Laplace Transform, Ch. II §5, Thm 5b) with a residue argument and a measurable density; not literally Montgomery–Vaughan's Lemma 15.1
literature.comparison: Montgomery–Vaughan (Multiplicative Number Theory I, §15.1, Lemma 15.1, p. 463) treat a locally Riemann-integrable density of eventually constant sign; the Lean lemma assumes only measurability and the bound |E(v)| ≤ C·e^v of IsPolar, and its meromorphic transform with prescribed residues. Widder's Theorem 5b (p. 58) gives the singularity at the real point of the abscissa for the increasing primitive of the nonnegative density K·e^(βv) − E(v)·e^v; the passage to that density, and the sign argument (the residue there is real and ≥ 0, while its value −r(a) has real part ≤ 0, so the singularity is removable), are separate steps.

imports.name: summable_taylor_of_removable
imports.lean:
lemma summable_taylor_of_removable {Ψ ε} {a z : ℂ} σ (D :
  AnalyticOnNhd ℂ (fun z ↦ (z - a) * Ψ z) (ball z ε)) (u : z ≠ a ∧ a ∈ ball z ε ∧ σ ∈ ball z ε) :
  Summable fun k ↦ (k ! : ℂ)⁻¹ • (σ - z) ^ k • iteratedDeriv k Ψ z := (hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball
  ((differentiableOn_dslope (isOpen_ball.mem_nhds u.2.1)).2 D.differentiableOn) u.2.2
  ).summable.congr (by erw [(eqOn_dslope_sub_smul ..).iteratedDeriv_of_isOpen isOpen_ne · u.1])
imports.text: If (z − a)Ψ(z) is analytic on the open disc of radius ε about z₀, z₀ ≠ a, and a, σ lie in that disc, then the Taylor series ∑_k (σ − z₀)^k Ψ^(k)(z₀)/k! converges (is summable). Ψ is a function defined at a, so (z − a)Ψ(z) vanishes at z = a; hence Ψ agrees off a with a function analytic on the whole disc (its slope at a, Mathlib's `dslope`), with the same derivatives at z₀ — the singularity at a is removable — and the Taylor series at z₀ converges on the disc.
